text: Assumption 1 . $\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ are i.i.d. samples with $x_{i}\sim N(0,I_{d})$ , and when conditioning on $x_{i}$ , $y_{i}\sim{\rm Bernoulli}(s(x_{i}^{\top}\theta^{*}))$ for some $\theta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.$
Assumption 2 . $\theta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is an unknown fixed parameter satisfying $\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}\geq 1$ .

Theorem 1 (Small stepsize GD) . Under Assumptions 1 – 2 , for any $\eta\in[0.1,7.9]$ , there exist some universal constants $C,c,\tilde{C}>0$ such that the following holds. If $\displaystyle n\geq C\Big(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{6}d\log n+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{6}\log\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}\Big),$ (2) then with probability at least $1-2e^{-d}$ , $\{\theta_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}$ generated by Algorithm 1 with $\theta_{0}=0$ and stepsize $\eta$ satisfies $\displaystyle\|\theta_{t}-\theta^{*}\|_{2}\leq\bigg(1-\frac{c}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}}\bigg)^{t}\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}+\tilde{C}\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}d}{n}},\quad\forall t=0,1,\cdots.$ (3)

Remark 1 . To our best knowledge, the only existing estimation guarantee of GD with logistic loss is [ 19 , Theorem 1] for bounded designs (i.e., $\|x_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1$ ), and our Theorem 1 provides the first non-asymptotic estimation error rate to GD in logistic regression with Gaussian designs. We believe that there are major differences between Gaussian designs and bounded designs, for instance, the bounded designs bypass the curse of dimensionality and as a result $d$ does not appear in their error rate. Moreover, a naive comparison finds that our Theorem 1 offers the following improvements: (i) Our error decay rate $O(n^{-1/2})$ is faster than their $O(n^{-1/4})$ ; (ii) To attain the final error rates our iteration complexity is $\tilde{O}(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3})$ while theirs reads $\tilde{O}(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}\sqrt{n})$ .

Remark 2 . Theorem 1 is also interesting from the optimization aspect in terms of the fast linear convergence in parameter. Specifically, recent works [ 35 , 18 , 30 ] also established the convergence of $\theta_{t}/\|\theta_{t}\|_{2}$ to a specific point, but the convergence rates, such as $O(\frac{\ln\ln t}{\ln t})$ from [ 18 , Theorem 1] , are much slower than ours. More are known about convergence in loss, such as the decreasing logistic loss with rate $E(\theta_{t}):=L(\theta_{t})-\min_{\theta}L(\theta)=O(\frac{1}{t})$ [ 31 ] , a comparable $E(\theta_{t})=O(\frac{\log^{2}t}{t})$ of recent work [ 18 ] , and the more recent linear convergence $E(\theta_{t})<0.1\min_{\theta}L(\theta)+\varepsilon$ whenever $t=\Omega(\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon})$ [ 3 ] . In light of a standard estimate $\mathcal{L}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta^{*})\leq\frac{1}{8}\|\theta-\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}$ (where $\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}L(\theta)$ is the population risk), our Equation ( 3 ) immediately yields the linear convergence in excess risk $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})-\mathcal{L}(\theta^{*})\leq\bigg(1-\frac{c^{\prime}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}}\bigg)^{t}\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}+C^{\prime}\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}d}{n},\quad\forall t=0,1,\cdots.$ (4) We expect that $\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})-\mathcal{L}(\theta^{*})$ is comparable to $L(\theta_{t})-\min_{\theta}L(\theta)$ up to some concentration error terms and $\mathcal{L}(\theta_{mle})-\mathcal{L}(\theta^{*})=O(d/n)$ [ 7 , Theorem 1] . Therefore, our linear convergence in risk is comparable to [ 3 ] and faster than [ 31 , 18 ] .

Theorem 2 (Large stepsize GD) . Under Assumptions 1 – 2 , there exist some universal constants $c_{0},c,C,\tilde{C}>0$ such that the following holds. Fix any $\eta>0$ such that $\displaystyle\frac{c}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}q^{\prime}(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})}<\eta<\frac{2-c\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{-2}}{m(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})}$ (5) where $m(\tau)=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)]$ , $q(\tau)=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}[s(\tau g)g]$ and $q^{\prime}(\tau)=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)g^{2}]$ , if $\displaystyle n\geq C\bigg(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{6}d\log n+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{7}d\bigg),$ (6) then with probability at least $1-2e^{-d}$ , $\{\theta_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}$ generated by Algorithm 1 with $\theta_{0}\in\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}(\theta^{*};\frac{c_{0}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}})$ and stepsize $\eta$ satisfies $\displaystyle\|\theta_{t}-\theta^{*}\|_{2}\leq\bigg(1-\frac{c}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}}\bigg)^{t}\frac{c_{0}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}+\tilde{C}\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}d}{n}},\quad\forall t=0,1,\cdots.$ (7) Moreover, a specific stepsize $\eta=\frac{1}{m(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})}$ satisfies ( 5 ).

Remark 3 . [ 41 ] first showed that large stepsize GD minimizes logistic loss and attains $E(\theta_{t})=L(\theta_{t})-\min_{\theta}L(\theta)=O(1/t)$ , then [ 40 ] provided finer optimization-theoretic characterizations and established a faster convergence $E(\theta_{t})=\tilde{O}(1/t^{2})$ (cf. their Corollary 2). See also further developments using adaptive stepsizes [ 44 ] or in a regularized setting [ 42 ] . While the faster convergence is commonly uncovered as a benefit of large stepsize, we emphasize that the settings in this line of works and in our paper are essentially different: [ 41 , 40 , 44 , 42 ] assume bounded covariates and separable data with margin $\gamma$ (see, e.g., [ 40 , Assumption 1] ), while we treat Gaussian designs and, under the sample complexity ( 6 ), our data $\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is provably non-separable (cf. [ 7 , Theorem 1] ). A naive comparison finds that our ( 8 ) is faster than [ 41 , 40 ] and comparable to [ 44 ] using adaptive large stepsizes. Concerning large stepsizes, there is an essential difference between separable data and non-separable data [ 38 , 42 ] : for linearly separable data the logistic loss is minimized at infinity, which enables arbitrarily large stepsize (e.g., [ 40 ] ); in contrast, under non-separable data (and mild condition) logistic loss admits a finite, unique minimizer, thus the GD iterates are necessarily unstable if $\eta$ exceeds some threshold [ 15 ] . Indeed the behaviors of large stepsize GD in non-separable data are much more intricate, for instance, under $d\geq 2$ , it was shown [ 29 , Theorem 3] that GD with $\eta=c\|\nabla^{2}L(\theta_{mle})\|_{op}^{-1}$ , $c\in(0,1]$ may converge to a stable cycle. Our Theorem 2 complements the negative results of [ 29 ] with a positive radius- $\Theta(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{-1})$ local convergence under Gaussian designs. Finally, while the different assumptions may forbid a close comparison, we again emphasize that the finite-sample statistical rate, $O_{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}(\sqrt{d/n})$ , is unique to our paper (see also Remark 1 ).

Lemma 1 . [ 26 , Corollary 7 & Theorem 5] Under Assumptions 1 – 2 and fix some $T_{0}\geq\log_{2}\log_{2}\frac{n}{d}$ , if $n\geq Cd\polylog n$ with large enough universal constant $C$ , then with probability at least $1-e^{-n}$ , $\hat{r}_{T_{0}}$ obtained by running $\tilde{r}_{t+1}=\hat{r}_{t}-\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\frac{\sign(x_{i}^{\top}\hat{r}_{t})+1}{2}-y_{i}\big)x_{i},~\hat{r}_{t+1}=\frac{\tilde{r}_{t+1}}{\|\tilde{r}_{t+1}\|_{2}},~~t\geq 0$ (or equivalently, Equation ( 11 ) below) with an arbitrary $r_{0}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ satisfies $\displaystyle\bigg\|\hat{r}_{T_{0}}-\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}\bigg\|_{2}\leq\polylog(n)\bigg(\sqrt{\frac{d}{n\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}}+\frac{d}{n}\bigg).$ (9)

Theorem 3 (Performance of Algorithm 2 ) . Under Assumptions 1 – 2 , if $n\geq\polylog n\big(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{4}\big)$ then with probability at least $1-n^{-1}$ , $\hat{\theta}$ obtained by Algorithm 2 with $T_{0}\geq\log_{2}\log_{2}\frac{n}{d}$ , $\hat{r}_{0}=(1,0,\cdots,0)^{\top}$ and $\nu\in[0.1,0.9]$ satisfies $\displaystyle\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{*}\|_{2}\leq\polylog(n)\cdot\bigg(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d}{n}}+\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}d}{n}\bigg).$ (12)

Remark 4 . Note that the rate ( 12 ) improves on the best known rate, the $O(\sqrt{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}d/n})$ for MLE [ 21 , 7 ] , as long as $\polylog(n)\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\leq\sqrt{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}d/n}$ , or equivalently, $d\geq\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}\polylog(n)$ , which covers most high-dimensional regimes of interest. Similarly, it improves on our GD rate, $O(\sqrt{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}d/n})$ , whenever $d\geq\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}\polylog(n)$ .

Remark 5 . Equation ( 12 ) reduces to $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d/n})$ whenever $\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}+\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}d}{n}\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d}{n}}$ , or equivalently, $n\gtrsim\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}d+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}.$ In this regime, the rate $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d/n})$ achieved by Algorithm 2 is nearly sharp in light of a matching lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d/n})$ . In fact, suppose that $\tilde{\theta}$ is an estimator for $\theta^{*}$ , then $\tilde{\theta}/\|\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}$ is an estimator for $\theta^{*}/\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}$ and therefore performs no better than an existing lower bound $\|\frac{\tilde{\theta}}{\|\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}}-\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}\|_{2}\gtrsim\sqrt{\frac{d}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}n}}$ [ 16 , Theorem 1] ; combining with a known bound $\|\frac{\tilde{\theta}}{\|\tilde{\theta}\|_{2}}-\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}\|_{2}\leq\frac{2\|\tilde{\theta}-\theta^{*}\|_{2}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}$ (e.g., [ 26 , Fact 13] ), we obtain $\|\tilde{\theta}-\theta^{*}\|_{2}\gtrsim\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d}{n}}$ . Therefore, we conclude that the tight error rate in the regime of $n\gtrsim\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}d+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}$ scales as $\sqrt{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d/n}$ . Nonetheless, the fundamental question of the optimal rate under $n\lesssim\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}d+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}$ remains open.

Remark 6 . We mention that Algorithm 2 generalizes to high-dimensional sparse case where the true parameter $\theta^{*}$ is $k$ -sparse. To that end, we only need to incorporate a hard thresholding operator into ( 11 ); see [ 26 , Algorithm 1] . Under $m=\tilde{\Omega}(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}k+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{4})$ , this sparse counterpart of Algorithm 2 achieves $\tilde{O}(\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}k}{n}}+\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}k}{n})$ . In contrast, it appears to be much harder to extend Theorems 1 , 2 to the sparse case.

Lemma 2 (Bounding $T_{c1}$ via covering) . There exist universal constants $C,c>0$ such that, for every $\delta\in(0,1)$ , with probability at least $1-\delta$ , $\left\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(s(x_{i}^{\top}\theta^{*})-y_{i}\big)x_{i}\right\|_{2}\leq C\left[\sqrt{\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{n\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}}+\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{n}\right].$

Lemma 3 (Bounding $T_{c2}$ via peeling) . For $u\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , define $Z_{n}(u):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(s(x_{i}^{\top}u)-s(x_{i}^{\top}\theta^{*})\big)x_{i}-\mathbb{E}\big[\big(s(x^{\top}u)-s(x^{\top}\theta^{*})\big)x\big].$ Fix $0<\rho\leq 3\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}$ . Then there exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that, with probability at least $1-\delta$ , $\|Z_{n}(u)\|_{2}\leq C\left[\sqrt{\frac{d\log(Cn)+\log\!\left(\frac{\log_{2}(6\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}/\rho)}{\delta}\right)}{n}}+\frac{d\log(Cn)+\log\!\left(\frac{\log_{2}(6\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}/\rho)}{\delta}\right)}{n}\right]\max\{\|u-\theta^{*}\|_{2},\rho\}$ holds uniformly over all $u$ satisfying $\|u\|_{2}\leq 2\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}$ .

Lemma 4 ( $T_{2}$ is a contraction under small stepsize) . Let $F(z)=m(\|z\|_{2})z$ and $m(\tau)=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)]$ . Fix $0<\eta<8$ . Let $v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ satisfy $\|v\|_{2}=R\geq 1$ . For any $u\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ satisfying $\|u\|_{2}\leq 2R,$ we have that $\|\eta(F(u)-F(v))-(u-v)\|_{2}\leq\left(1-\frac{c\eta\left(2-\frac{\eta}{4}\right)}{R^{3}}\right)\|u-v\|_{2}.$

Lemma 5 (( AIC1 ) implies convergence) . Under ( 43 ) and ( AIC1 ), $\{\theta_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}$ generated by Algorithm 1 with $\theta_{0}=0$ (and the $\eta$ in ( AIC1 )) satisfies $\displaystyle\|\theta_{t}-\theta^{*}\|_{2}\leq\bigg(1-\frac{c^{\prime}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}}\bigg)^{t}\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}+\tilde{C}\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}d}{n}},\qquad\forall t=0,1,\cdots.$

Lemma 6 . There exist universal constants $c,c_{0},c_{1}>0$ such that the following holds. Let $v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ satisfy $R:=\|v\|_{2}\geq 1.$ If $\displaystyle\frac{c}{R^{2}q^{\prime}(R)}<\eta<\frac{2-cR^{-2}}{m(R)},$ (49) then for any $\|u-v\|_{2}\leq\frac{c_{0}}{R}$ we have $\left\|\eta(F(u)-F(v))-(u-v)\right\|_{2}\leq\left(1-\frac{c_{1}}{R^{2}}\right)\|u-v\|_{2}.$ Moreover, $\eta=\frac{1}{m(R)}$ is a specific choice satisfying ( 49 ).

Lemma 7 (( AIC2 ) implies convergence) . Under ( AIC2 ) and $\displaystyle n\gtrsim\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{7}d~~~\textrm{with large enough hidden constant}$ (66) $\{\theta_{0}\}_{t\geq 0}$ generated by Algorithm 1 with $\theta_{0}\in\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}(\theta^{*};\frac{c_{0}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}})$ (and the $\eta$ in ( AIC2 )) satisfies $\displaystyle\|\theta_{t}-\theta^{*}\|_{2}\leq\bigg(1-\frac{c^{\prime}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}}\bigg)^{t}\frac{c_{0}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}+\tilde{C}\sqrt{\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{5}d}{n}},\quad\forall t=0,1,\cdots.$

Lemma 8 . If $n\gtrsim d$ and $\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}\geq 1$ , then it holds with probability at least $1-n^{-2}$ that $\displaystyle\Big|\hat{v}^{\top}\hat{r}-q(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})\Big|\leq\polylog(n)\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+\frac{d}{n\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}+\frac{d^{2}}{n^{2}}\bigg).$ (71)

Lemma 9 . Assume that the event ( 71 ) in Lemma 8 holds, i.e., $\displaystyle\Big|\hat{v}^{\top}\hat{r}-q(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})\Big|\leq\polylog(n)\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+\frac{d}{n\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}+\frac{d^{2}}{n^{2}}\bigg).$ (79) Under $\displaystyle n\geq\polylog(n)\bigg(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{4}+\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}d\bigg)$ (80) we have $\displaystyle|\hat{\lambda}-\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}|\leq\polylog(n)\bigg(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}+\frac{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}^{2}d}{n}\bigg)$ (81)

Lemma 10 (Stein identities [ 37 , 36 ] ) . Let $g\sim N(0,1)$ and let $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be absolutely continuous with $\mathbb{E}|\phi^{\prime}(g)|<\infty,~\mathbb{E}|g\phi(g)|<\infty.$ Then $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[g\phi(g)]=\mathbb{E}[\phi^{\prime}(g)].$ (89) Moreover, let $x\sim N(0,I_{d})$ and let $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously differentiable with $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|_{2}<\infty,~\mathbb{E}\|x\Phi(x)\|_{2}<\infty.$ Then $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[x\Phi(x)]=\mathbb{E}[\nabla\Phi(x)].$ (90) In particular, for $\Phi(x)=f(x^{\top}\theta)$ , $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[xf(x^{\top}\theta)]=\mathbb{E}[f^{\prime}(x^{\top}\theta)]\theta,$ (91) provided both sides are well-defined.

Lemma 11 . [ 5 , Theorem 2.10] Let $X_{1},...,X_{n}$ be independent random variables, and assume that for some $v,c>0$ , $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}X_{i}^{2}\leq v,$ $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}|X_{i}|^{q}\leq\frac{q!}{2}vc^{q-2},\quad\textrm{for all integers }q\geq 3,$ then we have $\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}X_{i})\bigg|\geq\sqrt{2vt}+ct\bigg)\leq 2\exp(-t),\quad\forall t>0.$

Lemma 12 . [ 39 , Theorem 2.8.1] Let $X_{1},...,X_{N}$ be independent, zero-mean, sub-exponential random variables. Then for every $t\geq 0$ , for some absolute constant $c$ we have $\mathbb{P}\left(\Big|\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}\Big|\geq t\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-c\min\Big\{\frac{t^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|X_{i}\|_{\psi_{1}}^{2}},\frac{t}{\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\|X_{i}\|_{\psi_{1}}}\Big\}\right)$

Lemma 13 . [ 39 , Theorem 7.3.1 & Corollary 7.3.3] Let $X\in R^{n\times d}$ be a matrix with independent $N(0,1)$ entries. Then $\mathbb{E}\|X\|_{op}\leq\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{d}$ and $\mathbb{P}\bigg(\|X\|_{op}\geq\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{d}+t\bigg)\leq 2\exp(-ct^{2}),\quad\forall t\geq 0.$
Lemma 14 . For $s(a)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-a}}$ , we have $s^{\prime}(a)=\frac{e^{-a}}{(1+e^{-a})^{2}}=s(a)\big(1-s(a)\big)$ and $\sup_{a\in\mathbb{R}}|s^{\prime}(a)|\leq\frac{1}{4}$ .

Lemma 15 (Order of $m(\tau)$ and $q^{\prime}(\tau)$ ) . Let $g\sim N(0,1)$ and $\displaystyle m(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)],$ $\displaystyle q(\tau)=\tau m(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[\tau s^{\prime}(\tau g)]=\mathbb{E}[s(\tau g)g].$ Then, for all $\tau\geq 0$ , $m(\tau)\asymp\frac{1}{1+\tau},\qquad q^{\prime}(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)g^{2}]\asymp\frac{1}{(1+\tau)^{3}}.$
Lemma 16 (Comparing $m(\tau)$ and $q^{\prime}(\tau)$ ) . Define $m(\tau)$ and $q^{\prime}(\tau)$ as in Lemma 15 . We have $m(\tau)>q^{\prime}(\tau),\quad\forall\tau>0.$

Lemma 17 (Upper bound on $\mathbb{E}(s^{\prime}(\tau g)|g|^{q})$ ) . For every integer $q\geq 3$ and every $\tau\geq 1$ , $\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}\big[s^{\prime}(\tau g)|g|^{q}\big]\leq\frac{2q!}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\tau^{q+1}}.$

Lemma 19 (Upper bound on $m^{\prime}(\tau)$ ) . For $m(\tau):=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)],$ we have $|m^{\prime}(\tau)|\lesssim\frac{1}{\tau^{2}},\qquad\tau\geq\frac{1}{2}.$
Lemma 20 (Upper bound on $q^{\prime\prime}(\tau)$ ) . For $q(\tau)$ defined in Lemma 15 , we have $|q^{\prime\prime}(\tau)|\lesssim\frac{1}{\tau^{4}},\qquad\tau\geq\frac{1}{2}.$

Lemma 21 . Let $q(\tau)$ be defined as in Lemma 15 . $q(\tau)$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$ and satisfies $q(0)=0,\qquad\lim_{\tau\to\infty}q(\tau)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$ Consequently, $q$ admits an inverse on $(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}),$ which we denote by $q^{-1}:(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}})\to(0,\infty)$ .
Lemma 22 . Let $q(\tau)$ be defined as in Lemma 15 . For every $\tau\geq 1/2$ , $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}-q(\tau)\asymp\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}.$

Lemma 23 . Under Assumptions 1 – 2 , we have $v=\mathbb{E}[y_{i}x_{i}]=q(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}},$ where $q(\tau):=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}[s(\tau g)g].$ Note that by Stein’s identity $q(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[\tau s^{\prime}(\tau g)]$ and thus coincides with the definition in Lemma 15 .
